content.p: The Zodiac Killer has never been identified. Between December 1968 and October 1969 someone shot or stabbed seven people in the northern San Francisco Bay Area, five of whom died, and then began writing to newspapers and telephoning the police to claim the attacks. He signed with a circle crossed by two lines, called himself "Zodiac", demanded that his coded messages be printed, and said he had killed far more people than police had counted. The letters kept coming into the 1970s. More than half a century later, no suspect has ever been charged, and the FBI told Fox News in October 2021 that its investigation "remains open and unsolved".

The case has outlived most of the people who worked it. It inspired the 1971 film Dirty Harry and later David Fincher's 2007 film Zodiac, and it keeps producing claims of a solution. The two that have mattered most are very different in kind: in December 2020 amateur codebreakers read a cipher that had defeated everyone for 51 years, and in October 2021 a private group announced a name that police promptly declined to endorse.

On the night of Friday 20 December 1968, two high school students, David Faraday, 17, and Betty Lou Jensen, 16, parked on Lake Herman Road in Benicia at the end of their first date. They had been to a Christmas concert at their school and had promised Betty Lou's parents they would be home by 11. A passing driver saw the couple's Rambler at the lovers' lane spot, and then another driver saw two bodies by the road. Betty Lou was dead with five bullet wounds in her back. David had been shot in the head and was still breathing, but he died. Bullet holes in the roof and back window of the car suggested the attacker may have fired warning shots to drive them out. Shell casings identified the ammunition as Winchester Western Super X, fired from a .22-caliber pistol. Investigators believed the teenagers were random targets killed by a stranger for no known reason.

Six and a half months later, shortly after midnight on 5 July 1969, Darlene Ferrin, 22, a married waitress and new mother, was sitting in her car with a friend, Michael Mageau, 19, in the parking lot of Blue Rock Springs Park in Vallejo. A second car pulled in, left, and came back to park behind them. A man carrying a light walked up and opened fire with a 9mm pistol. Mageau was hit in the face, neck and chest and survived. Ferrin was pronounced dead on arrival at the hospital. Mageau later described his attacker as a stocky white man of about 26 to 30, with short, light brown curly hair, according to the Independent.

About 45 minutes later a man telephoned Vallejo police, according to the Independent, and gave directions to the scene. HISTORY quotes him as saying: "I want to report a murder. If you will go one mile east on Columbus Parkway, you will find kids in a brown car. They were shot with a 9-millimeter Luger. I also killed those kids last year. Goodbye." Ferrin's sister Pam Huckaby, who was leaving the park as the killer's car arrived, told the Daily Democrat on the 50th anniversary that her family never learned who it was: "Our parents died not knowing who killed their oldest daughter."

The third attack came on the early evening of Saturday 27 September 1969 at Lake Berryessa in Napa County. College students Bryan Hartnell, 20, and Cecelia Shepard, 22, were picnicking when a man wearing a black hood with a white crossed-circle on the chest approached with a gun. He said he was an escaped prisoner who needed money and a car, and he had Shepard tie her companion's wrists with pre-cut plastic clothesline. He then stabbed Hartnell six times and Shepard ten. With a felt-tip pen he drew the crossed-circle on Hartnell's car door, with the dates of the earlier attacks and the words "by knife". A man telephoned the Napa County sheriff's office from a pay phone to report what he had done. The Independent says the call came from a car wash 27 miles away, that the receiver was found still dangling, and that a palm print was recovered but never matched. Shepard died two days later. Hartnell lived.

The fourth came two weeks after that. On Saturday 11 October 1969 a taxi driver, Paul Stine, was shot in the head in the Presidio Heights district of San Francisco. The Independent gives his age as 29 and HISTORY as 28. The killer took a piece of his shirt. Three witnesses described the man to police, but the dispatcher recorded the suspect as black, and two patrol officers let a white man leaving the area walk past without being questioned. A sketch was circulated but produced no match. The shooting was treated as a robbery until the Chronicle received a letter opening, "I am the murderer of the taxi driver", with a bloodied piece of Stine's shirt inside.

The correspondence began on 31 July 1969, when three near-identical letters, postmarked that day, went to a Vallejo daily and to the two big San Francisco papers, the Chronicle and the Examiner. Each contained the writer's claim to the shootings and one third of a cipher, and the letter to the Chronicle demanded publication by Friday 1 August. A longer letter to the Examiner, sent after police asked the writer for proof, was the first to use the name "the Zodiac". HISTORY says the Examiner received it on 4 August; the Independent dates it 7 August and quotes its opening: "Dear Editor This is the Zodiac speaking."

After the Stine killing the letters turned to threats. The Chronicle received a letter postmarked 13 October 1969 that mocked police and threatened to shoot children on a school bus. In one dated December 1969, addressed to the lawyer Melvin Belli, the writer said he feared he would kill again. In March 1970, Kathleen Johns, a young mother with a baby daughter, was driving near Modesto when a man pulled alongside, told her a wheel was loose and later offered her a lift to a gas station. She escaped with her child, and at a police station she recognised the Stine sketch as the man. A letter in July 1970 claimed that encounter. In another letter, in June 1970, the writer claimed to have shot a police officer, Richard Radetich, 25, in a parked car; the Independent notes that Radetich's killing was still unsolved in 2021.

The last letters HISTORY lists run to 1974 and include the "box score" line "Me - 37, SFPD - 0", read as a claim of 37 victims. The Independent says no murder between then and March 1971 can be definitively attributed to him. HISTORY lists other cases with signs of his hand, among them the Lake Tahoe disappearance of a nurse, Donna Lass, in September 1970, whose name was added to the list of possible victims after postcards were read as hints of a victim there. Her body was never found.

Zodiac sent four coded messages, and what they revealed is a measure of how little the case has yielded. The first, Z 408, was split into three parts and mailed to the three newspapers with the first letters. A schoolteacher, Donald Harden, and his wife Bettye, of Salinas, solved it within about a week, according to HISTORY; Bettye guessed it would begin with "I" and contain a form of "kill". The text said, in part, "I like killing people because it is so much fun." It also said he would be reborn in paradise and that his victims would become his slaves, and it explicitly withheld his name.

The second, Z 340, was postmarked 8 November 1969 and sent to the Chronicle with a greeting card and another piece of Stine's shirt. For 51 years nobody could read it, though the FBI had tried, and reports suggest the NSA and Navy cryptographers did too. In December 2020 David Oranchak, a software developer in Virginia, Sam Blake, a mathematician in Australia, and Jarl Van Eycke, a programmer in Belgium, announced the solution, and the FBI confirmed it. According to a paper the three released in 2024, Van Eycke's software AZdecrypt, and a new feature that inserted word breaks into candidate texts, were instrumental, and the three stress the long crowd effort behind the result.

The message does not name him. It begins, "I hope you are having lots of fun in trying to catch me", denies being the man who appeared on a television show, a reference to a caller in October 1969, and says that he is not afraid of the gas chamber because he now has "enough slaves to work for me" in paradise. Global News reported that the FBI told the San Francisco Chronicle it would not comment further because of the ongoing investigation. The bureau's spokeswoman Cameron Polan, quoted by the Guardian, said the Zodiac Killer case remained an ongoing investigation for the San Francisco division. The Guardian reported that the bureau said the solution did little to help investigators.

The other two have not been broken. Z 13, which follows the words "My name is", is short enough to allow several readings. The cryptologist Craig Bauer, writing for HISTORY, says he believes the right one spells Alfred E. Neuman, the Mad magazine mascot. Z 32 came with a map centred on Mt. Diablo, and the writer said it would show where a bomb was set.

Police have never charged anyone. The Independent reports that in 1991 Mageau identified a police suspect, Arthur Leigh Allen, as his attacker, and that Robert Graysmith's 1986 book and the film based on it point toward Allen, who died in 1992 before he could be questioned again. HISTORY records a different case in which police at one stage looked at a former lover of Bates's whom they described as jilted for the unsolved 1966 murder of Cheri Jo Bates in Riverside, a killing the Zodiac himself hinted at in a 1971 letter; DNA from hairs in Bates's hand did not match that man, who denied involvement. Riverside police say the Bates case is not connected to the Zodiac.

On 6 October 2021 a group of private investigators calling itself the Case Breakers, which described itself as former law enforcement officers, journalists and military intelligence officers, named Gary Francis Poste as the Zodiac. Poste was a housepainter and Air Force veteran who died in 2018. According to the group, the evidence included DNA, photographs from a darkroom in his home showing forehead scars that match a 1969 sketch, a Timex watch recovered from a crime scene, matching boot prints and, reportedly, an alternate message that appears when his name is applied to a cipher. The group also attributed the Bates killing to him.

The response from officials was swift. The FBI's San Francisco office said the case remained open and unsolved, and declined further comment. Vallejo police said they could neither confirm nor deny the report and would announce any major development. TheWrap quoted Riverside police officer Ryan Railsback, who told the Chronicle that the Case Breakers' material was circumstantial: "It's not a whole lot." Railsback told Fox News, "We 100% believe our Cheri Jo Bates case is not affiliated with the Zodiac case." KRON4 reported that the department said it knew of no physical evidence of the kind the group claimed and asked anyone with Zodiac tips to contact the FBI instead.

The group said in November 2021 that five police and state agencies had refused to cooperate with it, and announced that old associates of Poste said he had given away more than a thousand items, including weapons, pistol parts, powder and ammunition, which the group said could be evidence. Its leader, Thomas Colbert, boxed up the material, the group said, to send to private labs. CBS13 noted that in 2018 Vallejo police had sent two Zodiac letters to a private lab for DNA analysis; it is unclear whether usable results came back. Investigators were also reported to have renewed efforts using DNA-based ancestry databases, the method that led to the arrest of the Golden State Killer.
content.h2: Imitators and the cost to families
content.p: Global News notes that a copycat who used the Zodiac name and astrology signs in New York in the 1990s, Heriberto Seda, was identified and sentenced to life in prison. HISTORY counts three real-life copycats.

For the families, the long absence of an answer has been a private and sometimes intrusive burden. Huckaby told the Daily Democrat that reporters target her house and phone every year, that obsessive amateurs hound the family, and that she and her siblings once visited the doors of suspects themselves; she said she wanted the killer brought to justice in her lifetime. The case remains open with the FBI, and the Independent says the same of Riverside and Napa County.
